KEY MESSAGE 1... As of 2:55 PM EDT...Current sfc analysis shows
an elongated sfc low located over western NY and PA. This low 
has developed in response to an anomalous upper trough currently
seen on GOES 16 WV imagery over the Great Lakes. As this upper 
low closes off this evening and an upper shortwave tracks around
its southern periphery, a coastal low will form off the Mid 
Atlantic coast and eventually track near or over Long Island 
tonight into tomorrow, bringing periods of heavy rain and 
thunderstorms to the region. The sfc low and ULL both sit and 
spin overhead through Thursday, bringing continued showers to 
the region under the upper-level deformation axis. 

Current CIRA ALPW satellite imagery shows deep moisture surging
into the region this afternoon ahead of the approaching sfc low
aided by a strengthening southerly LLJ that will eventually 
turn to the southeast tonight and the east tomorrow. PWATs 
increase to 1.75 to 2.0 inches this afternoon into tomorrow, 
which is anomalous but not exceptionally so for late July. Warm 
cloud depths of around 12 kft will help to promote efficient 
warm rain processes, while unidirectional flow will promote 
backbuilding and training of storms. Mean cloud layer winds of 
only around 15 kt with slower MBE vectors will also support slow
storm motions. The strength of the forcing will be quite 
unusual, with MSLP and upper-level height anomalies as low as 
3-4 STD DEV below normal overlapping this very moist atmosphere.
Model forecast soundings continue to show a tall, skinny CAPE 
profile, with at least some elevated instability through 
Wednesday evening that will support the potential for heavy 
downpours. So, all signs are there for very heavy rain.

The location of the heaviest rainfall amounts will depend on 
exactly where training and backbuilding of convection sets up, 
which is still hard to determine several hours out from the 
heaviest rain. That said, we have seen a fairly large eastward 
shift with numerical guidance in the axis of heaviest QPF with 
this morning's 12z runs. Over the peaks and east-facing slopes 
of the Berkshires, E/SE upslope enhancement will likely lead to 
some rainfall totals of up to 3-5", with some higher amounts 
locally up to 7" not out of the question. Rainfall amounts have 
trended down slightly for the Mid Hudson Valley, and there may 
actually be some downsloping here off of the high terrain, but 
the Catskills are still expected to see up to 3-5" of rain with 
locally higher amounts up to 6-7" as well. Rainfall rates this 
afternoon and tonight are likely to exceed 1-2" per hour at 
times and may even briefly reach 3" per hour for a few areas in 
the Flood Watch. Rainfall rates tomorrow don't look quite as 
high as today, but could still exceed 1" per hour especially in 
southern VT and the Berkshires. With this rain tomorrow falling 
on already saturated soils, there will be a continued flash 
flood threat into tomorrow. 

Given the changes in expected QPF, we have expanded the flood watch 
into southern VT in coordination with WFO BTV. WPC has also expanded 
the day 1 moderate risk ERO into this area, and has introduced a day 
2 moderate risk ERO for much of our western New England areas while 
maintaining the marginal to slight for eastern NY. If some of these 
high-end rainfall amounts are realized, then numerous instances of 
flash flooding and some significant flash flooding will be possible. 
Local research has shown that many of our summer days featuring 
widespread flash flooding are associated with an upper lows like the 
one that will be overhead tonight and Wednesday, so this has added 
to our confidence in the potential for flash flooding. While many 
areas have been quite dry recently and could use some rain, this 
looks like a classic case of too much rain too quickly. 

Some lingering showers are expected Thursday, but are not expected 
to result in additional flooding. A dry period is then expected for 
Friday and Saturday, with increasing chances for rain again Sunday 
or Monday ahead of the next approaching upper trough and cold 
frontal system. 

Finally, will mention a low threat for some stronger storms this 
afternoon. Low-level and deep-layer wind shear are weak, but latest 
SPC mesoanalysis shows 1000-1500 J/kg of MLCAPE across the region, 
with the highest values south and east of the Capital District where 
there have been more breaks of sun this morning. Therefore, we can't 
rule out a few instances of wet microbursts leading to damaging 
winds with any taller storms this afternoon. However, threat for 
severe weather is much less of a concern than that for heavy rain 
and flash flooding. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Latest HEFS (Ensemble River Forecasts) 
continue to show a low (generally <10-15%) chance for main stem 
river flooding with this event, likely due to antecedent dry 
conditions and rainfall deficits. That said, within-bank rises 
on most rivers, creeks, and streams are expected.
